sessions.text: Mimi uses eight quantizers [moshi §3.3.1 p.10]. At a sampling rate of 12.5 Hz this configuration yields a bitrate of approximately 1.1 kbps [moshi §3.3.1 p.10].

sessions.label: Helium size
sessions.question: How large is the Helium text model? How much text did the team use to train it?
sessions.text: The Helium language model has about 7 billion parameters [moshi §5.1 p.22][moshi §3.2.2 p.7]. It was trained on roughly 2.1 trillion text tokens [moshi §5.1 p.22]. The papers do not specify the exact number of distinct documents or the total raw text volume in bytes.

sessions.label: H-Net ratio loss
sessions.question: Why does H-Net use a ratio loss?
sessions.text: H‑Net introduces a ratio loss to steer the model toward a desired compression ratio and avoid degenerate outcomes where it either keeps almost all vectors (nullifying compute savings) or compresses too aggressively (losing essential information) [hnet §2.2.3 p.8]. The loss provides continuous feedback via the average boundary probability G, allowing the network to train toward target ratios even though the actual fraction of selected vectors F is nondifferentiable [hnet §2.2.3 p.8]. By coupling this ratio loss with the autoregressive prediction loss, H‑Net can preserve content‑adaptive compression, selecting vectors based on semantic importance rather than fixed patterns [hnet §2.2.3 p.8]. The papers do not discuss any additional reasons for using the ratio loss beyond guiding compression efficiency.

passages.text: Dynamic Chunking. H-Net’s core is a novel dynamic chunking (DC) mechanism which interfaces between the main network and the encoder/decoder networks, learning how to segment data while using standard differentiable optimization. DC is composed of two complementary new techniques: (i) a routing module which predicts boundaries between adjacent elements through a similarity score (ii) and a smoothing module which interpolates representations using the router’s outputs, attenuating the effect of uncertain boundaries a

Without explicit regularization, the model may converge to trivial solutions: either retaining nearly all vectors (negating computational benefits) or compressing excessively (losing critical information). Moshi is a multi-stream speech-to-speech Transformer model, which allows for full-duplex spoken dialogue with a user thanks to an innovative architecture summarized in Figure 1. Moshi is built on top of Helium, a text LLM which we build from scratch (Section 3.2), relying on high-quality text data to provide strong reasoning abilities to the model. We also propose Inner Monologue (Section 3.4.4), a training and inference procedure in which we jointly model text and audio tokens. This allows the model to fully explo

Moshi pre-training. Then, we initialize the Temporal Transformer in Moshi with Helium, while the Depth Transformer described in Section 3.4.1 is randomly initialized. We first train on the unsupervised audio dataset presented in Section 4.2, using a single stream of audio, with a batch size covering 16 hours of audio, each batch item consisting of a 5 mn sequence. We mask the corresponding text tokens with a probability of 30%. We randomize the delay between the text and audio tokens between -0.6 and +0.6 seconds.

sessions.label: Warmup steps, in a burst
sessions.blurb: 12 s waiting for the token budget
sessions.question: How many warmup steps did the Transformer team use for the learning rate?
sessions.text: The Transformer team used 4000 warmup steps for the learning‑rate schedule [transformer §5.3 p.7].

passages.text: We used the Adam optimizer [20] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98 and ϵ = 10−9. We varied the learning rate over the course of training, according to the formula: lrate = d−0.5 model · min(step_num−0.5, step_num · warmup_steps−1.5) (3) This corresponds to increasing the learning rate linearly for the first warmup_steps training steps, and decreasing it thereafter proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. We used warmup_steps = 4000.

We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. For our base models using the hyperparameters described throughout the paper, each training step took about 0.4 seconds. We trained the base models for a total of 100,000 steps or 12 hours. For our big models,(described on the bottom line of table 3), step time was 1.0 seconds. The big models were trained for 300,000 steps (3.5 days).
